Requests and work orders

Two records, on purpose. A request is what somebody saw. A work order is what the team agreed to do about it. Keeping them apart stops a passing remark from turning into an unplanned intervention.

Anyone on site can raise a request

Scanning the QR code on a machine opens the form: equipment, criticality, description, photo. Operators do not need an account, so faults get reported when they are seen.

The manager decides what happens

Requests queue as pending, approved, refused or flagged to schedule. Approving one turns it into a work order and links the two records together.

Sub-tasks and safety checklists

A work order carries its own steps, from isolation and lockout through diagnosis, repair and return to service. Checklists can require a yes or no answer and a comment before the job closes.

Hours and parts recorded as they happen

The technician logs time against the job and the parts pulled from the store. The stock movement is written at the same moment, so the shelf and the system agree.

The states a job passes through

  1. 01

    Request submitted

    Created against a machine with a criticality and a description. Reference in the DI-2026-###### series.

  2. 02

    Reviewed

    Approved, refused, or flagged as an intervention to schedule. The decision keeps the reviewer's name.

  3. 03

    Work order open

    Sub-tasks, checklists, assigned technician and due date. Reference in the OT series.

  4. 04

    Closed

    Hours logged, parts consumed, PDF produced, machine availability updated.
